title: Place Value and Decimals to Thousandths
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Mathematics 0096 · Stage 6 · Number
summary: Learn what every digit in a decimal is worth, how to multiply and divide by 10, 100 and 1000, and how to split and regroup decimals to thousandths — with worked examples and a Checkpoint-style quiz.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Understand and explain what each digit in a decimal is worth: tenths, hundredths and thousandths (6Np.01)
Use place value to multiply and divide whole numbers and decimals by 10, 100 and 1000 (6Np.02)
Understand and explain the value of each digit when you build up (compose), split (decompose) and regroup numbers, including decimals to thousandths (6Np.03)

blocks.text: Place value is the idea that a digit's **position** decides its **value**. The digit 5 is worth 500 in 527, but only 5 hundredths (0.05) in 3.152. Everything in decimals — rounding, ordering, adding, multiplying — depends on this page, so learn it well.
Key words

blocks.text: 1. The place value chart

Each column is worth **10 times** the column on its right, and **one tenth** of the column on its left. This pattern carries on past the decimal point. Here is the number 3527.416 in a place value chart:

items: 10 thousandths = 1 hundredth (10 × 0.001 = 0.01)
10 hundredths = 1 tenth (10 × 0.01 = 0.1)
So 1 = 10 tenths = 100 hundredths = 1000 thousandths.

blocks.text: **Reading decimals aloud.** Say the digits after the point one at a time: 3.416 is "three point four one six", **not** "three point four hundred and sixteen". You can also say it as a fraction: 3 and 416 thousandths.

**Zero as a placeholder.** 0.5, 0.05 and 0.005 are very different numbers. The zeros push the 5 into the hundredths or thousandths place. Zeros at the **end** of a decimal do not change its value: 0.5 = 0.50 = 0.500 (5 tenths = 50 hundredths = 500 thousandths).
**Decimals on a number line.** Between two tenths there are ten hundredths, and between two hundredths there are ten thousandths. Zooming in on a number line shows this:

blocks.text: 2. Multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1000
When you multiply or divide by 10, 100 or 1000, the **digits move** and the **decimal point stays where it is**. The digits keep their order; only their places change.

blocks.caption: 4.65 × 100 = 465: each digit becomes 100 times bigger.

blocks.text: **Method (numbered steps):**

items: Count the zeros: 10 → 1 place, 100 → 2 places, 1000 → 3 places.
Multiplying makes the number bigger, so move the digits to the **left**. Dividing makes it smaller, so move them to the **right**.
Fill any empty places between the digits and the point with zeros (4.65 × 1000 = 4650; 38 ÷ 1000 = 0.038).
Do not write zeros at the end of a decimal, or in front of a whole number: write 46.5, not 46.50, and 465, not 0465.
Check with a sense of size: × 1000 should give a much bigger number; ÷ 1000 a much smaller one.

rows: digits 2, 0, 5 move 3 places left; one zero fills the ones place

blocks.text: **Missing-number questions.** If 0.62 × ☐ = 620, look at how far the digits moved: the 6 moved from tenths to hundreds, which is 3 places, so ☐ = 1000. If ☐ ÷ 100 = 0.37, undo it: 0.37 × 100 = 37.
**Where you meet this:** changing units. 1 m = 100 cm, so 2.35 m = 2.35 × 100 = 235 cm. 1 kg = 1000 g, so 750 g = 750 ÷ 1000 = 0.75 kg.
3. Composing, decomposing and regrouping
**Decomposing** means writing a number as the sum of the values of its digits:

items: 40.507 = 40 + 0.5 + 0.007 (no ones and no hundredths, so there is nothing to write for them)

blocks.text: **Composing** is the reverse. Put each part in its place. Be careful when the parts are given in a mixed order: 9 + 0.03 + 0.5 = 9.53 (the 0.5 is tenths, the 0.03 is hundredths). Using a place value chart stops you writing 9.035.
**Regrouping** means exchanging one unit for ten of the next smaller unit (or ten for one bigger). The number stays the same — only the way we split it changes. Here are some ways to make 2.586:

rows: 1 one moved into the second part

blocks.text: **Counting how many tenths, hundredths or thousandths.** 2.37 = 23.7 tenths = 237 hundredths = 2370 thousandths. To find how many hundredths, multiply by 100; how many thousandths, multiply by 1000.

في الضرب أو القسمة على ١٠ و١٠٠ و١٠٠٠: العلامة العشرية ثابتة والأرقام هي اللي بتتحرك — شمال في الضرب، يمين في القسمة، بعدد الأصفار.

blocks.text: Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Write the value of the digit 8 in 14.386. [1 mark]

items: Name the places after the point: 3 is tenths, 8 is hundredths, 6 is thousandths.
8 hundredths = 8/100 = 0.08.

blocks.text: **Answer:** 0.08 (or 8 hundredths). **Common mistake:** writing "8" or "hundreds". Hundreds are on the left of the point; hundred**ths** are on the right.

items: (a) × 100: digits move 2 places left. 4 tenths become 4 tens, 7 hundredths become 7 ones → **47**.
(b) 0.47 → 470: the 4 moved from tenths to hundreds = 3 places → **1000**.
(c) ÷ 100: digits move 2 places right. 3 ones become 3 hundredths → **0.039**.

blocks.text: **Common mistake:** in (c), writing 0.39 (moving only one place) or 0.0039 (moving three). Count the zeros in 100: two.
**Worked example 3** — Write 7.062 as the sum of the values of its digits. [1 mark]

7 is ones, 0 is tenths, 6 is hundredths, 2 is thousandths. **Answer:** 7 + 0.06 + 0.002. The zero tenths add nothing, so you do not need to write + 0. **Common mistake:** writing 7 + 0.6 + 0.2 — the 6 is hundredths, not tenths.
**Worked example 4** — Complete these: (a) 5.43 = 4 + ☐ (b) 5.43 = 5 + 0.3 + ☐ [2 marks]

items: (a) Take 4 away from 5.43: 5.43 − 4 = **1.43**. (One of the ones has been regrouped into the second part.)
(b) 5.43 = 5 + 0.43. You already have 0.3, and 0.43 − 0.3 = **0.13**. (One tenth was regrouped as 10 hundredths: 0.1 + 0.03 = 0.13.)

blocks.text: **Check:** 4 + 1.43 = 5.43 ✓ and 5 + 0.3 + 0.13 = 5.43 ✓. Always add your parts back together to check.
**Worked example 5** — A pack of 1000 sheets of paper is 94 mm thick. How thick is one sheet? Give your answer in mm. [1 mark]
One sheet = 94 ÷ 1000. The digits move 3 places to the right: 94 → 9.4 → 0.94 → 0.094. **Answer:** 0.094 mm. **Check:** 0.094 × 1000 = 94 ✓.
**Worked example 6** — Sara says: "To multiply by 10 you just add a zero, so 2.5 × 10 = 2.50." Is she correct? Explain. [1 mark]

**Answer:** No. 2.50 has the same value as 2.5, so adding a zero after the decimal part changes nothing. When you multiply by 10 the digits move one place to the left: 2 ones become 2 tens and 5 tenths become 5 ones, so 2.5 × 10 = 25. ("Add a zero" only works for whole numbers, such as 25 × 10 = 250.)

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Mixing up tens and tenths, hundreds and hundredths. If it ends in **-ths**, it is after the decimal point.
"Adding a zero" or "moving the point" with decimals. Think: the point stays, the digits move.
Moving the digits the wrong number of places: count the zeros in 10, 100 or 1000.
Forgetting the placeholder zero: 38 ÷ 1000 is 0.038, not 0.38.
Composing parts in the order they are written: 9 + 0.03 + 0.5 is 9.53, not 9.035.
Thinking 0.125 is bigger than 0.5 because 125 is bigger than 5. Compare place by place: 1 tenth is less than 5 tenths.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Write the value of the digit …" — give the value (0.08), not just the place name, unless the question asks for the place.
Missing-number boxes: 0.6 × ☐ = 600, or ☐ ÷ 100 = 0.35. Work out how many places the digits moved, or use the inverse.
Completing a partition: 4.276 = 4 + 0.2 + ☐ + 0.006, or a regrouped one such as 4.276 = 4 + 0.1 + ☐ + 0.006 (answer 0.17).
"Ring the number that is 100 times smaller than …" or matching lines between calculations and answers.
Reading a point on a number line that goes up in hundredths or thousandths: first work out what one small interval is worth.
"Explain why … is wrong" — name the place values in your explanation ("the 5 is in the tenths place, so …").
Paper 1 has no calculator, so you must be quick and accurate with × and ÷ by 10, 100 and 1000 in your head.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Place value and decimals — practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, from easy to Checkpoint-hard. No calculator. Type numbers only (no units). For the explain question, write your answer and mark it with the mark scheme.

questions.q: What is the value of the digit 7 in 5.374?
questions.e: After the point: 3 is tenths, 7 is hundredths, 4 is thousandths. So the 7 is worth 7 hundredths = 0.07.

questions.q: Which number has the digit 5 in the thousandths place?
questions.e: The thousandths place is the third place after the point. 2.415 → 5 ✓. 2.541 → 1; 5.124 → 4; 2.154 → 4.
× 100: digits move 2 places left. 4 tenths → 4 tens, 8 hundredths → 8 ones. 0.48 × 100 = 48.
÷ 100: digits move 2 places right. 4 tens → 4 tenths, 5 ones → 5 hundredths, 2 tenths → 2 thousandths. 45.2 ÷ 100 = 0.452.
The 2 moved from the ones place to the thousands place: 3 places left, so you multiplied by 1000. Check: 2.5 × 1000 = 2500.

questions.q: Write 6 + 0.4 + 0.009 as a single decimal number.
questions.e: 6 ones, 4 tenths, 0 hundredths, 9 thousandths → 6.409. The 0 is a placeholder for the hundredths.
The digit 8 is in the hundredths place, so its value is 0.08. Check: 3 + 0.5 + 0.08 + 0.002 = 3.582.

questions.q: Which of these is equal to 4.06?
questions.e: 40 tenths = 4 and 6 hundredths = 0.06, so 4 + 0.06 = 4.06 ✓. The others: 4.6, 40.6 and 0.46.

questions.q: How many hundredths are there in 2.37?
questions.e: 2 ones = 200 hundredths, 3 tenths = 30 hundredths, plus 7 hundredths: 200 + 30 + 7 = 237. (Or 2.37 × 100 = 237.)

questions.p: Ali thinks of a number. He divides it by 100 and gets 0.059.
questions.e: Use the inverse: 0.059 × 100. The digits move 2 places left: 5 hundredths → 5 ones, 9 thousandths → 9 tenths. Ali's number is 5.9. Check: 5.9 ÷ 100 = 0.059 ✓.

5.316 − 5 − 0.006 = 0.31. We have 0.2 of it, so the box is 0.31 − 0.2 = 0.11 (1 tenth was regrouped as 10 hundredths, plus the 1 hundredth). Check: 5 + 0.2 + 0.11 + 0.006 = 5.316 ✓. 1 mark for a method such as 0.31 − 0.2.

questions.q: Sami says: "3.4 × 10 = 3.40, because when you multiply by 10 you add a zero." Explain why Sami is wrong and give the correct answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: a correct explanation, e.g. 3.40 has the same value as 3.4 / adding a zero after a decimal does not change it / when you multiply by 10 the digits move one place to the left (3 ones become 3 tens, 4 tenths become 4 ones). 1 mark: correct answer 34. Do not accept 'move the decimal point' with no further reason for the explanation mark unless it says the number must get 10 times bigger.
questions.e: Writing 3.40 does not change the value (3.4 = 3.40), so it cannot be 10 times bigger. The digits move one place left: 3 ones → 3 tens, 4 tenths → 4 ones. 3.4 × 10 = 34.

blocks.title: Remember
items: After the point: tenths (0.1), hundredths (0.01), thousandths (0.001). Each place is 10 times the place on its right.
× 10, 100, 1000: digits move 1, 2, 3 places left. ÷ 10, 100, 1000: digits move 1, 2, 3 places right. The point stays still.
Use zeros as placeholders (0.038, 4050), but zeros at the end of a decimal change nothing (0.5 = 0.50).
Decompose by the value of each digit: 6.284 = 6 + 0.2 + 0.08 + 0.004.
Regroup by exchanging: 1 = 10 tenths, 0.1 = 10 hundredths, 0.01 = 10 thousandths. Always add your parts back to check.
